title: UK crypto de-banking hits 10,000 complaints; HKMA STR quality findings still open
summary: UK banks face a surge of 10,000 crypto-restriction complaints in one quarter, putting de-banking practices under dual regulatory fire. Plus: the HKMA STR quality thematic is still open for roughly a quarter of supervised institutions, and two Hong Kong CDD deadlines are closing fast.
script:
ALEX: Ten thousand complaints in a single quarter. That is the number that landed from the UK Financial Ombudsman Service on crypto-related de-banking, and I want to use it as a lens on something that matters to every APAC MLRO, not just the UK ones. Because the de-banking question is coming to every jurisdiction that has a live VASP population, and the UK is simply further along the curve.

JORDAN: I'll take that framing, but I want to push on something first. Ten thousand complaints in three months is not primarily a compliance story. It is a political story that is about to become a compliance story. The sequence matters. When complaints hit that volume, regulators do not just investigate the banks. They start asking whether the risk frameworks that produced those decisions were proportionate in the first place.

ALEX: That is a fair distinction. The Financial Conduct Authority and the Payment Systems Regulator in the UK are both looking at this, and the framing from supervisors there is very specifically around whether banks are applying blanket restrictions by customer type rather than individual risk assessment. That is the phrase that should make every head of financial crime compliance uncomfortable, because blanket-by-type is the opposite of risk-based.

JORDAN: And here is where I will partially disagree with you, Alex. You are framing this as if the banks are obviously in the wrong, and I do not think that is the fair read from the front line. If your correspondent banking relationships are conditioning their access on your crypto exposure, and your own AML framework has not caught up with the FATF Recommendation 15 virtual asset guidance, the path of least resistance for a risk team is to restrict. That is not laziness. That is a resource and clarity problem.

ALEX: That is a genuine point, and I take it. But the supervisory response to "we restricted because it was easier" is not going to be sympathetic. The direction of travel from every regulator I am watching, whether it is the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, or AUSTRAC in Australia, is that a risk-based approach means you must be able to show individual assessment. The complaints volume in the UK is going to accelerate that expectation everywhere.

JORDAN: Agreed on the direction. So the practical question for an MLRO in this region is: can you actually demonstrate, transaction by transaction or customer by customer, that your decisions on crypto-related payments are individually reasoned and documented? Because that is what an examiner is going to ask for, and "we apply a category restriction to all VASPs" will not be a sufficient answer for much longer.

ALEX: So what should listeners do with this?

JORDAN: If you are the MLRO at a bank that is restricting crypto-related transactions at a category level, you need to do two things before end of week. First, pull your current policy and check whether it can demonstrate individual risk reasoning, or whether it is effectively a blanket rule dressed in risk-based language. Second, check your complaint data. If you are seeing an uptick in complaints specifically about payment restrictions on crypto, that is a lead indicator that your examiners will eventually see the same pattern you are. Get ahead of it. Brief your head of retail banking and your risk committee before they read about it elsewhere.

ALEX: Good. Moving on to the HKMA obligation picture, because there are three items in the active queue that deserve attention right now. The overdue item is the more urgent one. The HKMA ran a thematic review of suspicious transaction report narrative quality across its supervised authorized institutions in late 2025, and deficiency letters went out to roughly a quarter of the population in early 2026. The closure of those findings is technically overdue as of April, and for any institution that received a letter and has not formally closed the finding, that is an open regulatory commitment sitting on the table.

JORDAN: I want to be blunt about this one, because I think some institutions are treating these deficiency letters as a paperwork exercise rather than a substantive one. STR narrative quality is not a peripheral issue. It is the thing that determines whether a financial intelligence unit can actually use the information you file. If your STR describes a transaction as "unusual activity inconsistent with customer profile" and stops there, you have technically filed a report and substantively filed nothing.

ALEX: The HKMA's concern, based on the thematic framing, is exactly that. The quality gap they identified was around specificity of grounds, the description of the specific conduct that triggered the suspicion, not just the fact that suspicion existed.

JORDAN: And I would add that this matters doubly right now because the December deadline for periodic customer due diligence reviews of high-risk customers under Section 16 of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance is approaching. If you are refreshing high-risk CDD and the review surfaces a materially changed transaction pattern, you are back in STR territory. So the quality of your STR governance and the quality of your CDD refresh are linked in a way that is worth making explicit to your team.

ALEX: There is also the annual AML/CFT self-assessment return to the HKMA under Guideline 11, which was due in September. If that has slipped or is pending sign-off, it should be prioritised immediately.

JORDAN: The Australian listeners have their own equivalent pressure point. The annual board-level review and approval of the AML/CTF Program under Section 84 of the AML/CTF Act had a deadline of the end of August. If that board sign-off is sitting in a draft pack waiting for a November meeting, it is already overdue. AUSTRAC does look at whether the board actually approved the program, not just whether compliance prepared one.

ALEX: So before we close, the through-line today is proportionality and documentation. Whether it is crypto payment restrictions in the UK rippling toward APAC practice, STR narrative quality in Hong Kong, or annual program approvals in Australia, the supervisory question in every case is the same: can you show your reasoning, specifically, at the level of individual decisions?

JORDAN: If any of that felt uncomfortably close to your own queue, that is the point. The full obligation register with source links for every item we have discussed today is at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. See you tomorrow.
